title: A King Was Told to Strike the Ground With His Arrows. He Stopped Too Soon—and Elisha Became Angry.
paragraphs:
A King Was Told to Strike the Ground With His Arrows. He Stopped Too Soon—and Elisha Became Angry.
Joash had arrows in his hand, a promise from God in front of him, and a dying prophet beside him. Then he stopped after three strikes. What happened next should terrify anyone who has ever mistaken partial obedience for finished faith.
There are moments in Scripture that make you uncomfortable because they feel too familiar.
Not because you have stood beside the deathbed of Elisha.
Not because you are the king of Israel.
Not because Syria is waiting outside your borders.
But because you know what it feels like to stop.
To pray until nothing seems to change.
To fight until fighting becomes exhausting.
To believe boldly at first…and then quietly lower your expectations.
To obey God, but only so far.
To take three swings when perhaps you should have kept striking.
And sometimes the most dangerous sentence in the Christian life is not, “I don’t believe God.”
There is a strange, almost painfully human scene buried in 2 Kings 13.
Elisha—the prophet through whom God had performed extraordinary works—is dying.
The man who had watched Elijah disappear into heaven.
The man associated with the multiplying of a widow’s oil.
The man through whom God raised the Shunammite woman’s son.
The prophet whose ministry had confronted kings, armies, famine, idolatry, unbelief, and death itself…
Scripture does not romanticize the moment.
“Now Elisha was fallen sick of his sickness whereof he died” (2 Kings 13:14, KJV).
Even people mightily used by God eventually discover that the human body cannot be negotiated with forever.
And into that room comes Joash, king of Israel.
“My father, my father, the chariot of Israel, and the horsemen thereof.”
Those words are striking because they echo what Elisha himself had cried when Elijah was taken from him in 2 Kings 2:12.
Joash seems to understand that Israel is about to lose more than an old man.
Yet there is an uncomfortable tension in the scene.

Joash reigns over a kingdom whose spiritual condition is deeply compromised. Earlier in the chapter, Scripture says he “did that which was evil in the sight of the LORD” and did not depart from the sins of Jeroboam (2 Kings 13:11).
He can mourn a prophet while ruling without wholehearted covenant faithfulness.
Because it is possible to admire holy things without surrendering to the Holy One.
It is possible to cry during worship and return unchanged.
To quote Scripture and still protect the sin Scripture confronts.
To love sermons about Jesus while refusing the Jesus those sermons proclaim.
To be emotionally moved by God without being spiritually yielded to God.
Then the dying prophet gives the king an unusual command.
Then Elisha places his hands upon the king’s hands.
The trembling hands of a dying servant of God resting upon the hands of a ruler who will soon have to fight without him.
Then Elisha tells him to open the east window.
“The arrow of the LORD’S deliverance, and the arrow of deliverance from Syria.”
An arrow of victory—deliverance belonging to the LORD.
The arrow did not contain divine power.
Elisha was giving Joash a prophetic sign attached to the word of the LORD.
Israel’s deliverance would not ultimately come from Joash’s bow.
Because Scripture does not teach us to place faith in rituals, objects, formulas, symbolic gestures, “prophetic techniques,” or human performance.
The sign mattered because God’s word gave the sign its meaning.
Elisha tells Joash that he will strike the Syrians at Aphek until they are consumed.
The moment Joash could never take back.
And suddenly the dying prophet is angry.
“And the man of God was wroth with him.”
“Thou shouldest have smitten five or six times; then hadst thou smitten Syria till thou hadst consumed it: whereas now thou shalt smite Syria but thrice.”
Joash was not condemned because three was some forbidden number.
Scripture does not tell us that Elisha had secretly instructed him to strike exactly six times.
Nor does the passage explicitly tell us what Joash was thinking when he stopped.
We should not pretend to know what God did not reveal.
Did he simply assume three strikes were enough?
But it does reveal the consequence.
He stopped sooner than Elisha expected, and the limited striking corresponded to limited victories.
That is where this ancient king suddenly gets uncomfortably close to us.
Because maybe you know something about stopping too soon.
You opened your Bible determined to change.
You wanted to forgive someone who wounded you.
You wanted to rebuild your relationship with Christ.
Started confessing things you had hidden for years.
And somewhere inside your heart came the whisper:
Still knew when to say amen.
Still looked Christian enough from the outside.
Your arrows were lying on the ground.
There is something deeply unsettling about Joash’s story because he did obey.
And that is precisely why this story can expose something we would rather hide:
Sometimes we are willing to obey God as long as obedience does not require endurance.
A strong marriage without dying to selfishness.
Freedom from sin without cutting off what keeps feeding the sin.
A powerful prayer life without putting down the phone.
Biblical understanding without opening the Bible.
A transformed life without surrendering the life we already built.
Then look toward heaven as if to say:
But do not turn this passage into a prosperity formula.
It is not teaching that if you repeat a prayer six times instead of three, God must give you your desired outcome.
It does not promise that persistence guarantees the career, relationship, money, healing, child, ministry, or earthly breakthrough you want.
Some prayers are answered differently than we hoped.
Paul pleaded three times concerning his thorn, and instead of removing it, Christ answered:
“My grace is sufficient for thee: for my strength is made perfect in weakness” (2 Corinthians 12:9).
So biblical perseverance is not manipulating God until He gives us what we demand.
It is refusing to abandon God when He does not.
Faith does not say, “God owes me victory because I struck the ground enough times.”
“Even when I cannot understand what God is doing, I will keep trusting the God who has already revealed Himself in Jesus Christ.”
That is where this story becomes bigger than Joash.
The king loses the man he called “my father.”
But God does not die with Elisha.
In fact, immediately after Elisha’s death, Scripture records one of the strangest miracles in the Old Testament.
A dead man is thrown into Elisha’s grave.
And the man revives and stands upon his feet.
Even at the grave, God is reminding Israel:
My power did not die with My servant.
Then the narrative returns to Syria.
“And the LORD was gracious unto them, and had compassion on them, and had respect unto them, because of his covenant with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob” (2 Kings 13:23).
Joash was not presented as a model of wholehearted faithfulness.
That is the heartbeat beneath the battlefield.
And centuries later, grace would step onto another battlefield entirely.
Jesus Christ came into a world filled with people who had stopped too soon, failed too often, sinned too deeply, hidden too long, promised too much, and obeyed too little.
When obedience became painful, He did not stop.
When His disciples fled, He did not stop.
When Peter denied Him, He did not stop.
When soldiers mocked Him, He did not stop.
When nails pierced His hands, He did not stop.
When darkness covered the land, He did not climb down from the cross.
“Christ became obedient unto death, even the death of the cross” (Philippians 2:8).
And when His saving work reached its appointed completion, Jesus cried:
Joash’s limited striking was followed by limited victories.
Christ’s finished work accomplished what sinners could never accomplish for themselves.
And the Gospel is not that exhausted sinners must strike the ground hard enough to earn God’s love.
The Gospel is that Christ has done what sinners could never do.
You are not saved by how many arrows you strike.
You are saved by grace through faith in Jesus Christ.
“For by grace are ye saved through faith…not of works” (Ephesians 2:8–9).
But the grace that saves us also changes us.
It teaches us to get back up.
Because His blood has already purchased redemption.
Not to make God love us.
Because in Christ, grace has already come looking for sinners.
We persevere because Jesus is worth following.
Maybe that is what somebody reading this needed tonight.
You prayed longer than anybody knows.
You smiled while your faith was bleeding internally.
And eventually you put the arrows down.
“God, I don’t know if I can do this anymore.”
Your hope is not your ability to manufacture one more heroic burst of religious energy.
Pick the arrows back up—not because your striking saves you, but because Jesus has not abandoned you.
Delete what keeps pulling you toward sin.
Call the person you need to forgive.
Seek reconciliation where reconciliation is biblically possible.
Ask Christ to expose what you have been protecting.
And when you fall, do not turn your fall into your permanent address.
There may also be someone reading this who has never truly surrendered to Christ.
Maybe you grew up with it.
Being near the things of God is not the same as belonging to Christ.
Joash could weep over Elisha while still being described as a king who did evil before the LORD.
That should sober every religious heart.
You can be moved without being transformed.
So stop hiding behind Christianity and come to Christ.
The person you became when nobody was watching.
Because the cross was never designed for people pretending they had no scandal.
Jesus Christ died for sinners and rose again.
There is reconciliation with God in Him.
There is no sin made clean by hiding it, but there is no repentant sinner beyond the sufficiency of Christ’s grace.
That is why we keep saying it:
Not by pretending the scandal never happened.
Jesus rewrites everything by taking guilty people, washing them through His blood, forgiving them by grace, making them His own, and teaching them to walk in newness of life.
Maybe your story currently looks like three arrows lying in the dirt.
That does not have to be the final scene.
And please do not keep this article trapped on this page.
Not because sharing a post earns favor with God. It does not.
Not because clicking “share” proves you are a better Christian. It does not.

But if this truth can reach one exhausted believer, one wandering son, one ashamed daughter, one collapsing marriage, one person secretly returning to an addiction, one lukewarm Christian, one skeptic willing to reconsider Jesus, or one sinner wondering whether grace could possibly still have their name on it—why would we want to keep it to ourselves?

If you want to glorify God, let that desire become more than emotion. Support Gospel-centered work that faithfully points people toward Christ. Share biblical truth. Help put Scripture in front of people who may never walk through a church door on their own. Send this privately to someone you know is fighting quietly.
It is not buying spiritual favor.
It does not make God love you more.

It is simply a practical way to support the work while receiving deeper biblical nourishment, discipleship, encouragement, accountability, and spiritual sharpening as we keep pointing people toward Jesus.
Send it to the person who walked away.
Invite the person who thinks their scandal disqualified them forever.
Because perhaps somewhere tonight there is a person holding the last arrow they thought they had.
Perhaps they were about to put it down.
Perhaps God will use one verse, one testimony, one shared article, one friend refusing to remain silent, to turn their eyes back toward Christ.
Your story is still being written.
And if you belong to Jesus, the Author holding your life is not finished with His work in you.
when shame tells you to disappear…
when your past starts screaming your old name…
Then look at the empty tomb.
Grace has already walked into places darker than yours.
Do not let the sound of the arrows you dropped become louder than the voice of the Savior who finished what you never could.
